extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and exercises about finiteness/Noetherian hypotheses, schemes over rings (A-schemes), finite type, varieties, normality/integral closedness, factoriality/UFD, and associated primes/points and rational functions in the setting of schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducedness is stalk-local
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducedness is a stalk-local condition: X is reduced iff all stalks O_X,p are reduced (Exercise 5.2.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to check reducedness pointwise. Appears as a basic local criterion; referenced when comparing to other stalk-local properties (e.g., normality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian scheme: finiteness of irreducible components
rubrics_metrics.description: If a scheme X has underlying topological space that is Noetherian, then X has finitely many irreducible components; if two of them meet at a point p, then O_{X,p} is not an integral domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can extend to locally Noetherian schemes by covering by open irreducible subsets. Some Noetherian hypotheses are necessary (see Stacks tag 0568).

rubrics_metrics.name: A-scheme (scheme over a ring A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-scheme (scheme over A) is a scheme where all rings of sections of the structure sheaf (over all open sets) are A-algebras, and all restriction maps are maps of A-algebras (equivalently the data of a morphism X -> Spec A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the relative notion used when working over a base ring/field such as C, Q, or Z. Later understood properly as a morphism to Spec A (Exercise references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally of finite type over A
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is an A-scheme covered by affine opens Spec B_i where each B_i is a finitely generated A-algebra, then X is locally of finite type over A (a locally finite type A-scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If furthermore X is quasicompact, X is of finite type over A. Over Noetherian base rings, schemes locally of finite type are locally Noetherian; finite type over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian. Key geometric examples: Spec C[x1,...,xn]/I and P^n_C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiprojective implies finite type (exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasiprojective A-scheme, then X is of finite type over A. If A is Noetherian, show X is Noetherian and has finitely many irreducible components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.D(a). Shows relationship between projectivity/quasiprojectivity and finite type; contains cautionary remarks about non-Noetherian bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open subschemes of projective schemes: local finite type and quasicompactness
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is an open subscheme of a projective A-scheme then U is locally of finite type over A; if A is Noetherian then U is quasicompact and hence quasiprojective and therefore of finite type over A. This can fail for non-Noetherian A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.D(b). Suggests constructing explicit counterexamples when A is not Noetherian (hint: Silly example 4.5.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine/projective variety (over k) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine scheme that is reduced and of finite type over k is an affine k-variety. A reduced (quasi)projective k-scheme is a (quasi)projective k-variety. (Warning: in some literature 'variety' also assumes irreducibility or k algebraically closed.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.E(a): Spec k[x1,...,xn]/I is an affine k-variety iff I is radical. Projective case has cautions about graded radical ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a closed point
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of a closed point p of a locally finite type k-scheme is the degree of the field extension κ(p)/k. If k is algebraically closed, every closed point has degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: points in A^1_k corresponding to irreducible polynomials have degree equal to the degree of that polynomial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytiﬁcation of complex varieties (exercise/warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X a reduced, finite type C-scheme, one can define a complex analytic prevariety X^{an} whose points correspond to closed points of X; the analytification should not depend on choice of affine cover and can be made functorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 5.3.G: requires familiarity with complex analytic varieties; warns nonisomorphic complex varieties can have isomorphic analytifications (except if compact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrally closed domain (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral domain A is integrally closed if the only zeros in K(A) to any monic polynomial in A[x] lie in A itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical example: Z. This property is preserved under localization (Exercise 5.4.A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal scheme (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is normal if all of its stalks O_{X,p} are normal, i.e., integral domains integrally closed in their fraction fields. Thus normality is a stalk-local property and implies reducedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normality can be checked on closed points for quasicompact schemes. Normal schemes need not be integral (e.g., disjoint union of normal schemes). See remarks and exercises for examples and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization test for integral closedness
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integral domain A, the following are equivalent: (i) A integrally closed; (ii) A_p integrally closed for all prime ideals p; (iii) A_m integrally closed for all maximal ideals m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 5.4.2 and its proof outline: integral closedness preserved by localization; if not integrally closed, use ideal of denominators to find a maximal m where A_m is not integrally closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factoriality (locally factorial) of schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is factorial if all its stalks are unique factorization domains (UFDs). (Sometimes called 'locally factorial'; note this notion is not affine-local.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: factorial does not imply there exists an affine cover by Specs of UFDs. Example: elliptic curves are factorial though no affine open is Spec of a UFD (reference Exercise 19.11.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization preserves UFD-ness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any nonzero localization of a unique factorization domain is a unique factorization domain (Exercise 5.4.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence if A is a UFD then Spec A is factorial. The converse need not hold (Exercise 5.4.N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to check a Noetherian domain is a UFD
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful methods: (0) elementary Euclidean algorithm cases and Gauss's Lemma for polynomial rings; (1) localization property (Exercise 5.4.E); (2) height 1 prime ideals are principal (Proposition 11.3.5); (3) normal and class group Cl = 0 (Exercise 14.2.T); (4) Nagata's Lemma (Exercise 14.2.U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution: some constructions (e.g., A[[x]]) may not preserve UFD-ness. Historical examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD implies integrally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Unique factorization domains are integrally closed; hence factorial schemes are normal (Exercise 5.4.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also notes existence of integrally closed rings that are not UFDs (Exercises 5.4.L, 5.4.K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and counterexamples for normality and factoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of normal schemes: A^n_k, P^n_k, Spec Z; examples and exercises exhibit rings that are integrally closed but not UFD (Z[√−5], cone over quadric), or schemes that are factorial though no affine open is Spec of a UFD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 5.4.H–5.4.N provide constructions and hints: quadratic extensions, diagonalizing quadratic forms, cone over quadric surface A = k[w,x,y,z]/(wz−xy), and base-change behavior of normality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated primes/points: geometric characterization (A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The associated primes/points of a module M (or of A) are precisely the generic points of irreducible components of the support of some element of M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property (A). Motivated by examples: Spec k[x,y]/(y^2, xy) has two associated points (generic point of x-axis and origin). This can be taken as definition in some contexts; in Noetherian setting it coincides with algebraic definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of associated primes (B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian ring A and finitely generated module M, M has a finite number of associated primes/points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property (B). Consequences: only finitely many irreducible closed subsets can appear as supports of elements; Noetherian hypotheses are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zerodivisor characterization via associated primes (C)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element f of A is a zerodivisor on M iff it vanishes at some associated point of M (i.e., lies in some associated prime of M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property (C). One direction follows from prior properties; this links algebraic notion of zerodivisor to vanishing on associated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization behavior of associated primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated primes/points behave well under localization: the associated primes of S^{-1}M are precisely the associated primes of M that lie in Spec S^{-1}A (i.e., do not meet S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important Exercise 5.5.F. This allows defining associated points of a locally Noetherian scheme by checking on affine neighborhoods; notion is stalk-local.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of (A)–(C) for locally Noetherian schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) A locally Noetherian scheme has finitely many associated points. (ii) Supports of functions are unions of closures of some subset of associated points. (iii) Generic points of irreducible components are associated points; others are embedded points. (iv) Reduced locally Noetherian schemes have no embedded points. (v) The nonreduced locus is the closure of associated points with nonreduced stalks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These consequences synthesize prior properties to give geometric control over functions, support, and nonreduced behavior. See Exercises 5.5.C–5.5.O for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injection of global sections into product of stalks at associated points
rubrics_metrics.description: For a locally Noetherian scheme X and open U, the natural map Γ(U, O_X) -> ∏_{p associated in U} O_{X,p} is injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displayed as (5.5.5.1) / (5.5.3.1). This gives that rational functions determined by values at associated points are unique and allows defining maximal domain of definition for rational functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational function (definition via associated points)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational function on a locally Noetherian scheme is an element of the image of Γ(U, O_X) in the product of stalks at associated points for some U containing all associated points; equivalently a section defined on some open containing all associated points, modulo agreement on overlaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently the colimit of O_X(U) over open sets containing all associated points. Rational functions have a maximal domain of definition, and are regular at points in that domain. If X is reduced, this coincides with being defined on an open set of each irreducible component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total fraction/quotient ring
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational functions form a ring, called the total fraction ring (or total quotient ring) of X; for X = Spec A affine this is the total fraction ring of A. If X is integral, this is the function field K(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extends the notion of field of fractions to reducible/nonintegral schemes using associated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic definition of associated prime (annihilator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime p ⊂ A is associated to an A-module M if p is the annihilator of some element m ∈ M (i.e., p = Ann(m) = {a ∈ A : a m = 0}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as definition (D) in the text; this algebraic notion is equivalent to the geometric description (A) in the Noetherian/finitely generated setting and is used to prove properties (A)–(C).
